# THE OLDEST CHINESE PRINTED WORK IN THE LIBRARY OF CONGRESS

This specimen, dated 975 A. D., is the earliest example of Chinese printing in the Library of Congress. It is a Buddhist invocation sutra recovered from the foundations of the famous Lei-fêng-t'a (Thunder Peak Pagoda), which for nearly 1,000 years stood on the banks of West Lake in Hangchow but which collapsed on September 25, 1924. A number of Buddhist sutras had been placed in hollow bricks when the pagoda was erected during the reign of Ch'ien Shu (929–88 A. D.), prince of the Kingdom of Wu-yüeh.

<summary>A historical description of the Library of Congress's oldest Chinese printed artifact, a 975 A.D. Buddhist invocation sutra retrieved from the ruins of the collapsed Thunder Peak Pagoda (Leifeng Pagoda) in Hangzhou.</summary>
<keywords>Chinese printing, early block printing, Library of Congress, Buddhist invocation sutra, Leifeng Pagoda, Lei-fêng-t'a, West Lake, Hangzhou, Ch'ien Shu, Kingdom of Wu-yüeh, 10th century, 975 A.D.</keywords>

# THE OLDEST CHINESE PRINTED WORK IN THE LIBRARY OF CONGRESS

This specimen, dated 975 CE, is the earliest example of Chinese printing preserved in the Library of Congress. It is a Buddhist invocation sutra <note>original: *dharani sutra*. A sacred text containing ritual incantations recited to generate spiritual protection and merit.</note> recovered from the foundations of the famous Leifeng Pagoda <note>original: *Lei-fêng-t'a* (Thunder Peak Pagoda). A prominent brick-and-wood pagoda erected on Sunset Hill along West Lake in Hangzhou.</note>, which stood on the shores of West Lake in Hangzhou <note>historically romanized as Hangchow; the capital city of modern Zhejiang province, China.</note> for nearly a millennium before its sudden collapse on September 25, 1924. Multiple Buddhist sutra scrolls were sealed within specially hollowed bricks when the pagoda was constructed under the auspices of King Qian Chu <note>reigned 948–978 CE; lived 929–988 CE, prince and final sovereign of the regional Wuyue Kingdom during the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms era.</note>, ruler of the Kingdom of Wuyue.

<summary>A curatorial identification label describing a 975 CE Buddhist invocation sutra scroll found sealed inside hollow bricks of Hangzhou's Leifeng Pagoda, recognized as the earliest specimen of Chinese woodblock printing held by the Library of Congress.</summary>
<keywords>Chinese printing, woodblock print, Buddhist invocation sutra, dharani, Leifeng Pagoda, Thunder Peak Pagoda, West Lake, Hangzhou, Qian Chu, Kingdom of Wuyue, Song Dynasty, Library of Congress</keywords>

## Illustration of Even-Hedged Mourning Attire (Qīshuāi tú)

<note>Qi shuai (齊衰) represents the second degree of ritual mourning garments in traditional Chinese rites, characterized by hemmed or even edges of coarse linen, distinct from the raw, unhemmed edges of the highest grade (Zhancui). In funeral rituals, it is typically accompanied by a square-bottomed ritual staff crafted from paulownia wood.</note>

<summary>This page presents the ritual diagram for Qi Shuai, the second-degree mourning attire worn in traditional Confucian bereavement rites, highlighting the prescribed hemmed garments and ceremonial staff.</summary>
<keywords>Qi shuai, mourning dress, ritual garments, Wufu, Yili, funeral rites, Confucian ritual</keywords>

<term>Iron Helmet<note>original: 頭鏊 (Tóu ào). # The Mechanical Raft
<term>xiefa</term> <note>original: 械筏; an engineered floating barrier or boom made of sharpened timber stakes bound together to obstruct enemy waterways or defend river approaches</note>

## Illustration of the Second-Degree Mourning Attire <note>Chinese: *Zishuai* (齊衰, also pronounced *Qishuai*). In traditional Confucian ritual systems documented in classics such as the *Book of Etiquette and Ceremonial* (*Yili*) and the *Classic of Rites* (*Liji*), this represents the second of the five mourning grades (*wufu*). The garment is sewn from coarse hemp with trimmed, even hems—distinguishing it from the untrimmed hems of the first grade (*zhancui*)—and is paired with a paulownia ritual staff with a square base.</note>

<summary>This page features a canonical woodcut illustration depicting the second-degree Confucian mourning attire (zishuai), showing the prescribed robes, headgear, and square-bottomed paulownia staff used in formal funeral rites.</summary>
<keywords>zishuai, second-degree mourning dress, Confucian ritual, five mourning grades, wufu, funeral rites, Book of Etiquette and Ceremonial, Classic of Rites</keywords>

# Newly Proposed Diagram of the Deep Garment

<note>original: 新擬深衣圖 (Xīn nǐ shēnyī tú) — "Newly Proposed Diagram of the Deep Garment." In Neo-Confucian scholarship, scholars frequently sought to reconstruct the exact patterns of ancient ritual attire based on classical texts like the *Classic of Rites* (Liji).</note>

### Technical Vocabulary

*   **Newly Proposed** <term>Xinni — Refers to a revised or updated scholarly reconstruction of an ancient standard or ritual object, re-evaluated according to classical commentaries.</term>
*   **Deep Garment** <term>Shenyi — The historic full-length robe of Chinese scholars and officials, composed of an upper garment (yi) and lower pleated skirt (chang) sewn together into a single robe, worn as formal civilian dress.</term>
*   **Collected Illustrations of the Three Realms** <term>Sancai Tuhui — An influential illustrated encyclopedia compiled by Wang Qi and his son Wang Siyi, published in 1609 during the Ming Dynasty, covering Heaven, Earth, and Humanity.</term>
*   **Clothing** <term>Yifu — The treatise section within the encyclopedia dedicated to ceremonial vestments, everyday dress, headwear, and regalia across Chinese history.</term>

<summary>This page illustrates a newly reconstructed pattern for the classical Deep Garment (Shenyi) from the Ming Dynasty encyclopedia Sancai Tuhui, serving as an important primary source for Neo-Confucian ritual dress.</summary>
<keywords>Sancai Tuhui, Shenyi, Deep Garment, Chinese costume history, Ming Dynasty encyclopedia, ritual attire, Neo-Confucian clothing</keywords>

# Portrait of Emperor Ming of Han
<note>original: 漢明帝像 (Hàn Míng Dì xiàng)</note>

<term>Emperor Ming of Han <gloss>The "Illuminated" or "Enlightened" Emperor of Han</gloss></term> <note>Reigned 57–75 CE; born Liu Zhuang (劉莊). The second emperor of the Eastern Han dynasty, he was the fourth son of Emperor Guangwu and Empress Yin Lihua.</note>

This woodblock print illustrates the likeness of <term>Emperor Ming</term>, shown seated in traditional imperial regalia. Renowned as an exceptionally diligent and exacting administrator, Emperor Ming upheld his father's policies of centralizing imperial power and revitalizing Confucian classical institutions, while enforcing the law with uncompromising severity.

In the illustration, the ruler is depicted wearing the ceremonial <term>mianguan</term> <gloss>beaded crown of state</gloss>, featuring a rectangular mortarboard with suspended rows of jade beads that signified clear moral vision and heavenly mandate. His formal court attire reflects the restored ceremonial codes and ritual revival of the early Eastern Han era.

According to prominent historical traditions, Emperor Ming's reign is celebrated for several monumental developments:
*   **The Introduction of Buddhism:** Tradition recounts that following an auspicious imperial dream of a golden divinity flying before his palace, Emperor Ming dispatched an imperial delegation to the Western Regions. This led to the arrival of the Indian monks Kasyapa Matanga and Dharmaratna, along with the translation of the *Sutra of Forty-Two Chapters* and the founding of the legendary White Horse Temple in Luoyang, marking the dawn of Buddhism in China.
*   **Administrative Diligence and Surveillance:** A meticulous sovereign, Emperor Ming closely monitored his court officials, rigorously checked administrative malfeasance, and suppressed royal clan rebellions, establishing a reign noted for domestic stability.
*   **Consolidation of the Northern Border:** Under his direction, Han armies successfully campaigned against the Northern Xiongnu, reopening the trade networks of the Silk Road through the Western Regions.
